0ac6227fa766d141: Fruity compounds such as isoamyl acetate (banana) and ethyl acetate (pear, solvent) made by yeast. Warmer, higher-gravity fermentations and low pitching rates raise them. Read the guide
f5aa3087279cb1bb: Tax charged by a state on alcohol made or sold within it, collected through permits, labels or volume-based charges. Structures and processes vary by state, so brewers need local advice. Read the guide
cfa1350750e48e88: Extra neutral alcohol Wine and spirits
a8457dfc6a44c395: Highly rectified spirit of about 95 to 96% ABV with little flavour of its own. In India it is the base of most mass-market spirits, usually made from molasses or grain. Read the guideAlso: ENA, neutral spirit
41267e1a13d32987: Dissolved solids, mostly sugars, in wort or released from malt. Malt specifications list extract as the percentage of dry weight a standard lab mash recovers. Read the guide
6099fd9cc7673856: Amino acids and small peptides in wort that yeast uses to build new cells. An all-malt wort usually has plenty; heavy adjunct use dilutes it and can stress the yeast. Read the guideAlso: Free amino nitrogen
84795476bf0d74d6: Goan spirit distilled from fermented cashew apple juice or coconut palm toddy, traditionally in small pot stills. Cashew feni holds a geographical indication tag.
0085ac31479d686c: Yeast turning wort sugars into alcohol, carbon dioxide and flavour compounds. Controlling its temperature does more for beer quality than almost anything else a brewer does. Read the guide
80416e6fb9dee57a: Level to which a bottle or can is filled, checked against the declared volume. Short fills shortchange the drinker and overfills waste beer, so lines check it every shift.Also: fill level
faa393518f2aca8f: Passing beer through a medium such as diatomaceous earth, sheets or membranes to remove yeast and haze. It gives bright, stable beer with a longer shelf life. Read the guide
ac1a2d0846256f26: Gravity once fermentation is complete. Together with original gravity it gives alcohol content through ABV = (OG - FG) x 131.25. Read the guideAlso: FG, Terminal gravity
127b18b1e6a40eea: Adding an agent such as bentonite, egg white or gelatin to wine so it binds haze-forming or harsh compounds that then settle out. Some agents make a wine unsuitable for vegans. Read the guide
26f8488e5b822258: Clarifying agents such as isinglass, gelatine or silica sol that bind to yeast or haze particles and drag them down. They speed up clarity without filtration. Read the guide
a39a69976c021853: Flavours and sensations left after swallowing, described as short or long, dry or sweet, bitter or clean. A good finish invites the next sip. Read the guideAlso: aftertaste
1a7a9df32553e303: Strongest, most concentrated wort drained from the mash before sparging begins. Its gravity tells you how well the mash converted. Read the guide
ac57f65ca079676e: Core beer a brewery is best known for and sells all year round. Its steady volume usually pays for the seasonal experiments. Read the guide
74223bd3ef0b54d4: Chart that groups beer flavour terms from broad classes at the centre to specific descriptors at the rim. It gives tasters and brewers a shared vocabulary. Read the guide
4f445f03869e1ae5: Tendency of yeast cells to clump together then drop out of suspension once fermentation slows. Highly flocculent strains clear quickly but may stop early, while low flocculators stay in suspension longer. Read the guide
d8a5f9b156105559: Film of yeast that grows on fino and manzanilla sherry in barrels left part full. It shields the wine from oxygen and gives a tangy, nutty, bread-dough character. Read the guide
6e64332297cc53f1: Tiny jet of hot water or CO2 squirted into a bottle just before capping so the beer foams up and drives air out of the headspace. It is a cheap way to cut oxygen pickup. Read the guideAlso: jetting
63874d1f6300f541: Test that stores sealed beer warm, commonly at 30°C (86°F) or higher, for days or weeks to predict how it will taste months later on the shelf. Read the guideAlso: accelerated ageing
0fdc25b946247ac4: Adding CO2 under pressure to cold beer in a tank or keg. It is faster and more controllable than natural carbonation. Read the guideAlso: Force carbonation
66395f82454c49a4: Adding grape spirit to wine during or after fermentation, raising alcohol to roughly 15 to 22% ABV. Port, sherry and Madeira are made this way. Read the guideAlso: fortified wine
81314e920092f927: India's national food regulator, which sets standards for alcoholic drinks covering composition, additives and labelling. Breweries need its licence alongside state excise approvals. Read the guideAlso: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
a64cdafc0ad8ef69: Heavier alcohols made by yeast that give hot, solvent-like warmth. Fermenting too warm or under-pitching increases them. Read the guideAlso: Higher alcohols, Fusels
1d2d2d76d49e82bf: Swelling and bursting of starch granules in hot water, which opens the starch to enzyme attack. Barley malt starch gelatinises at normal mash temperatures, whereas rice and maize need more heat. Read the guide
4bef16f3b065d8cb: Plant ingredients that flavour gin, led by juniper, which must dominate, plus coriander, citrus peel, angelica and many others. Indian gins often add local spices. Read the guideAlso: botanicals
229028ceb9a64d1e: Food-grade coolant chilled and pumped through tank jackets to hold fermentation and storage temperatures. A properly sized glycol system is essential in hot Indian conditions. Read the guideAlso: Glycol chiller
3251fa619186b8d1: Tart German wheat beer brewed with salt and coriander, first from Goslar and later Leipzig. Light and refreshing, it suits hot weather. Read the guide
3780014148bfaf91: Mixture of milled malt and other grains ready for mashing. The grist bill lists each grain with its share, usually given in recipes as percentages. Read the guideAlso: Grain bill, Grist bill
78a434b10043ca32: Revenue minus cost of goods sold, often shown as a percentage of revenue. It shows how much each sale contributes towards overheads and profit. Read the guide
639c4f2ca4855b88: Stage after the lag phase when yeast multiplies rapidly and ferments most of the sugar. Much of the beer's ester and fusel character forms here, so temperature control matters most. Read the guideAlso: Exponential phase, Log phase
1980eecfcf9e8b5d: Blend of young and old lambic, bottled so the young beer referments and builds a lively sparkle. It is dry, sour and complex. Read the guide
0fcaae0c83e79d53: Brewing salt that adds calcium plus sulphate, lowering mash pH and giving a crisper, drier hop finish. It is the classic addition for Burton-style pale ales. Read the guideAlso: Calcium sulphate
713357b84ab15072: Brewing by a brand or brewer with no plant of its own, renting spare capacity at other breweries batch by batch. It is a common way to test demand before investing. Read the guideAlso: cuckoo brewing, nomad brewing
ce623a4ff353433a: Total calcium and magnesium in water, usually given as mg/L of calcium carbonate. Calcium in particular helps enzymes, yeast flocculation and beer clarity. Read the guideAlso: Water hardness
85df1af0c11691e0: Cloudiness in beer from protein, polyphenols, yeast, starch or bacteria. Some styles want it; in a beer meant to be bright it is a stability fault. Read the guide
40a8a79b01fb4356: How long the foam on a poured beer lasts before collapsing. Grease, detergent residue on glasses or poor foam proteins can kill it quickly. Read the guide
509d2507291bbbc6: Gas space between the beer and the closure in a bottle or can. Air left there is a major source of package oxygen, so fillers work hard to push it out. Read the guide
0a379653439b265c: Stack of metal plates that cools hot wort against cold water or glycol flowing the other way. It brings wort to pitching temperature in one pass while recovering hot water. Read the guideAlso: Plate chiller, Wort cooler
fa667f69f5c55e2b: Unit of 100 litres, the standard way breweries express batch size, tank volume and annual output. A 10 hl brewhouse makes about 1,000 litres per brew. Read the guideAlso: hl
15a94920e7522ff9: Unfiltered Bavarian wheat beer with banana and clove aromas from its special yeast. It is usually at least half wheat malt and served cloudy in a tall vase-shaped glass. Read the guideAlso: Weissbier
c054139efe68e49b: Pale Munich lager that leans towards soft, bready malt rather than hop bitterness. Clean and gentle, it was created in 1894 as Bavaria's answer to pilsner. Read the guide
89f93c5b58eb33d6: Peak of fermentation, when the krausen is tallest and activity most vigorous. Brewers often time dry hopping, krausening and temperature changes around it. Read the guide
42e9e9c2f1dd8084: Harsh, scratchy, peppery feeling from hop particles left in suspension in heavily dry-hopped beers. Cold crashing and time help them settle. Read the guide
a084c3f21b2904c1: Renewed fermentation set off when enzymes in dry hops break dextrins into fermentable sugars. It can raise ABV, diacetyl and pressure in tanks or packages. Read the guide
dbdb01877649a24e: Hop resins and oils pulled out of the cone, usually with liquid or supercritical carbon dioxide. It gives precise, consistent bitterness with almost no vegetal loss in the kettle. Read the guideAlso: CO2 extract
92a2332c57c2137e: Volatile compounds in lupulin, a small fraction of the cone's weight, that carry most hop aroma. They boil off easily, which is why aroma hops go in late or after the boil. Read the guideAlso: Essential oils
83121f4c3218852f: Hops milled into powder then pressed into small pellets, usually labelled T90. They store better and take less space than whole cones, which is why most breweries use them. Read the guideAlso: T90 pellets
516a10e7df85ce29: Share of the alpha acids added that end up as iso-alpha acids in finished beer, typically well under half. Boil time, wort gravity and losses to trub and yeast all affect it. Read the guide
2ab27171b43f02fd: Cone-shaped flowers of the female hop plant, used for bitterness, aroma and flavour. Their resins also help protect beer against some spoilage bacteria. Read the guideAlso: Humulus lupulus
8032ac512c9599b1: Clumps of protein and polyphenol that coagulate early in the boil, often after a foamy surge. A good hot break helps clarity and flavour stability. Read the guide
006154fba87dbc9f: Insulated vessel that heats and stores brewing water for mashing in and sparging. Its size and reheat time often limit how many brews a day a brewhouse can run. Read the guideAlso: HLT
8840cc289fefcb35: Weighted glass float that measures the density of wort or beer by how deep it sinks. Brewers use it to track fermentation and work out alcohol content. Read the guide
14afc47a9c7c38a0: Lab measure of bitterness roughly equal to milligrams of iso-alpha acids per litre. It tracks bitter compounds but not how bitter a beer tastes against its malt. Read the guideAlso: International Bitterness Units
93578459157c9008: Label word for a stronger, more intense version of a style, as in imperial stout or imperial IPA. It signals more malt, more alcohol and usually more of everything. Read the guide
b06375924f1cac37: Strong, rich, dark stout, often 8 to 12% ABV, with intense roast, dark fruit and chocolate notes. It was historically brewed in London for export to the Russian court. Read the guideAlso: Russian imperial stout
62b8de1105713cfa: Mash held at a single temperature, usually somewhere in the 62 to 70 °C (144 to 158 °F) range, reached by adding hot water. It suits well-modified modern malts and is the simplest method. Read the guideAlso: Single infusion mash
8934f0bb9bdb0ce9: Hop-forward pale beer with more bitterness and hop aroma than a standard pale ale. Born in England, it now spans English, West Coast, hazy and double versions. Read the guideAlso: India pale ale
844714abea87c150: Chemical rearrangement of hop alpha acids into bitter, soluble iso-alpha acids during the boil. Longer boiling increases it, which is why bittering hops go in early. Read the guide
7d102bdf6b076d33: Sealed stainless steel container, commonly 20, 30 or 50 litres, that holds pressurised beer for draught dispense. Kegs protect beer from light and air far better than open vessels. Read the guide
59830f3739a77dce: Vessel where wort is boiled with hops, heated by steam jacket, internal calandria or direct fire. Many modern kettles double as whirlpools. Read the guideAlso: Copper, Brew kettle
6f9df94992edef0d: Drying germinated grain with hot air to halt growth and develop colour and flavour. Low temperatures give pale base malts; higher temperatures give Munich, Vienna and darker malts. Read the guide
f02ab908d96d0c82: Moment the boil ends and wort is sent through the heat exchanger into the fermenter. Knockout temperature should match the yeast's pitching temperature. Read the guideAlso: Casting
6fd3037ea0f2cabd: Pale, delicate beer from Cologne fermented with ale yeast at cool temperatures, then cold-conditioned. In Europe only Cologne-area brewers may use the name. Read the guideAlso: Kölsch
014abb57529d522c: Rocky head of foam, yeast and hop resin that forms on top of fermenting wort. It rises, peaks then falls back as fermentation moves through its phases. Read the guide
0a90d9bc0c6e4b2f: Norwegian farmhouse yeast cultures that ferment quickly and fairly cleanly at unusually high temperatures, often 30 to 40 °C (86 to 104 °F). They suit Indian breweries short on cooling capacity. Read the guide
a9d7e1df2daa7192: Process of getting a drink's label approved by the state excise department before sale. Each state reviews labels separately and requirements vary, so multi-state launches take time. Read the guideAlso: label registration
732fcded9e6a9aba: Rings of foam that cling to the inside of the glass as the beer is drunk. Good lacing suggests healthy foam proteins and a properly cleaned glass. Read the guideAlso: Brussels lace
3df5d225636e3b51: Quiet period after pitching while yeast absorbs oxygen and nutrients before visible activity starts. A long lag gives wild microbes time to get established. Read the guide
b4ce6ea7479cbc0e: Beer fermented with bottom-fermenting lager yeast at cool temperatures, then cold-conditioned. Lagers are usually crisp and clean; most beer sold in India is lager. Read the guide
553bf455cd22b774: Strains of Saccharomyces pastorianus that ferment cool, usually 8 to 13 °C (46 to 55 °F), for a clean profile with few esters. They tend to settle at the bottom of the fermenter. Read the guideAlso: Saccharomyces pastorianus, Bottom-fermenting yeast
a6ed4dc6e1fc7065: Cold storage of beer near freezing, often for weeks, after fermentation. It settles yeast and haze, smooths flavour and gives lagers their clean, crisp finish. Read the guide
6e6ebe60d3933c6d: Spontaneously fermented wheat beer from the Brussels region, cooled in open vessels so wild microbes settle in, then aged in wooden barrels for months or years. It is tart, funky and usually still. Read the guide
f79b4d8e144290ed: Wide, false-bottomed vessel where wort is separated from the grain bed, often with rotating rakes to keep the bed open. Its shape is built for clear, efficient runoff. Read the guide
9be9dd655f44b6fc: Separating the sweet wort from spent grain, using the husk bed as a filter. A slow, even runoff gives clear wort with good extract. Read the guideAlso: Wort separation
c620bb4a60fd4d47: Dead yeast and other sediment that settle after fermentation. Ageing wine on its lees, called sur lie, adds texture and bready complexity. Read the guide
30b01076bb9f06de: Annual or one-off fee paid to the state for the right to brew, store or sell alcohol. Licence categories, fees and renewal cycles vary by state. Read the guide
191de7ffa21426b9: Damage caused when blue and ultraviolet light breaks down hop bitter compounds in beer, creating a skunky smell. In clear or green glass it can happen within minutes in sunlight. Read the guideAlso: lightstruck
2ec5f22a17b19964: Limit of attenuation Fermentation and conditioning
4edc6f95ec703dfb: Lowest gravity a wort can reach, found by fermenting a sample warm with plenty of yeast. Comparing it with the tank shows whether a fermentation has truly finished.Also: Forced fermentation test, Fermentability
3178b3eea24aa7cf: Floral, citrusy hop alcohol found in most aroma hops, linked to orange and lavender notes. It survives fermentation better than many hop oils, making it a useful marker of hop aroma. Read the guide
41e1220ba0749d76: London dry gin Wine and spirits
920c76908572825d: Gin style where all flavour comes from botanicals distilled with the spirit, with only water and a trace of sugar allowed afterwards. The name describes a method, not a place. Read the guide
76e3f4a85c4d3710: Yellow, sticky glands inside the hop cone that hold the alpha acids, beta acids and essential oils. Almost everything a brewer wants from a hop sits in this powder. Read the guide
2df6ab77e56baaeb: Adjunct used as grits or flakes that lightens body while leaving a soft, faintly sweet corn note. Grits need cooking to gelatinise the starch; pre-gelatinised flakes can go straight into the mash. Read the guideAlso: Corn, Maize grits
ac31c8a119d20b9d: Conversion of sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid by bacteria, usually after the main ferment. It softens acidity and can add buttery notes to reds and some whites. Read the guideAlso: MLF, malo
311bbdb1f54f4b78: Grain, usually barley, that has been steeped, germinated and kilned so its starch and enzymes are ready for the mash. It supplies most of the sugar, colour and flavour in beer. Read the guide
5570efe99383a2ce: Controlled steeping, germination and kilning of grain to develop enzymes and soften the kernel. How the maltster runs it decides colour, flavour and how easily the malt converts in the mash. Read the guide
4bd1f5f50a0584de: Mixture of grist and hot water held at set temperatures so malt enzymes convert starch into sugars. Mash temperature and pH largely decide how fermentable the wort will be. Read the guide
39b402cd296a32e1: Raising the mash to about 76 to 78 °C (169 to 172 °F) at the end of mashing. It slows enzyme activity and thins the wort for an easier runoff. Read the guide
e7cabfdcc5e23d6d: Acidity of the mash, measured on a cooled sample, with 5.2 to 5.6 the standard target range. Within it enzymes work well, tannin extraction stays low and beer tastes cleaner. Read the guide
ef3dea7726873619: Vessel where grist and hot water are mixed and held for conversion. In simpler two-vessel brewhouses it also serves as the lauter tun. Read the guide
44c5f325317375a3: Time a spirit or wine spends ageing in cask, drawing flavour from the wood, oxidising gently and losing harsh notes. Heat speeds the process up. Read the guide
07235f1d9b4147ba: Tinny, blood-like or coin-like taste, usually from iron or other metal ions picked up from water, worn equipment or poorly passivated stainless steel. Read the guide
72141230afa9b862: Small brewery producing limited volumes, often with its own bar. In India the word often means an on-premise brewing licence; its exact meaning and rules vary by state. Read the guide
12cefb1bdec4e313: Crushing malt to crack the husk and expose the starchy interior while keeping husks largely whole. A good crush balances extract against a smooth, fast lauter. Read the guideAlso: Crushing
7a8dcd9bd92ce894: Extent to which malting has broken down the cell walls and proteins inside the grain. Well-modified modern malts convert easily in a single infusion mash, while undermodified malts benefit from step or decoction mashing. Read the guide
463f9ac4979e548c: Physical sensations a beer gives in the mouth, such as body, carbonation, warmth, creaminess and astringency. It shapes how refreshing or rich a beer seems. Read the guide
ba313966b88fea3c: Highest price at which a packaged product may be sold to consumers in India, printed on the pack. For alcohol it is also shaped by state excise pricing rules. Read the guideAlso: maximum retail price
a0fe11734483fe8a: Kilned base malt with deeper colour plus rich bready, toasty flavour, while keeping enough enzymes to convert itself. It adds malt depth to bock, Märzen and dunkel. Read the guide
a4d7386c4c8a29b3: Freshly crushed grape juice with its skins, seeds and pulp, before or during fermentation. Red wine takes its colour from fermenting with the skins in the must. Read the guide
e2579cf757f6512d: Usually the most abundant oil in hops, giving green, resinous and herbal aroma. It is very volatile, so it survives mainly in dry-hopped beers. Read the guide
aabad03b5d0912d8: Hazy, juicy IPA with soft bitterness, a full mouthfeel and heavy late hop additions. It stales quickly, so it is best drunk fresh and kept cold. Read the guideAlso: New England IPA, hazy IPA
